tagline.text: A 36-hectare forest eco-retreat in the Sierra Madre foothills near Manila

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Day trip or 2 days and 1 night

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~7,500 (from a day-visit entrance to one night in a room)

children.text: Purro Nature Reserve is a family-run forest sanctuary of about 36 hectares in the Sierra Madre foothills of Calawis, Antipolo. It is roughly 1.5 to 2 hours by car from Manila, so you can fit forest hikes, a river trek, a Dumagat cultural experience and a night of forest rest into one trip.
Purro Nature Reserve is a private forest sanctuary of about
36 hectares

in Barangay Calawis (Purok 5), Antipolo City, Rizal. It sits on the western foothills of the Sierra Madre, inside the Upper Marikina River Basin Protected Landscape. It takes its name from nearby Mount Purro, but the reserve is not on the summit itself; it lies on the lower slopes.

The reserve is run by the Malvar family. According to travel blog accounts, the owner began reforestation in nearby uplands in the 1990s and has planted more than 1,000 trees since then, and a place that started as a personal retreat was opened as a nature camp for families, friends and groups. It is not just a resort: its stated purpose is to restore the forest and support the livelihoods of upland communities, which makes it a true eco-retreat.
It is about
1.5–2 hours

by car from central Manila, so a day trip is possible, but a 2-day, 1-night stay in a forest cottage suits it best. There is no air conditioning, but the mountain breeze keeps things cool, and Wi-Fi and mobile signal are weak, so it is a place to unplug on purpose. Many rooms have open windows with mosquito netting, so you sleep to the sounds of the forest.

The trekking is not very demanding, so beginners and families with children can join, and activities include a zipline, a ropes course, a river trek, a Dumagat indigenous cultural experience and bonfires. Rates and package contents vary by season and booking method, so check the latest information on the official website or booking channel before you go.
The forest trail from the reserve up to Malvar's Peak is described as about
45 minutes–1 hour
one way, with an elevation gain of about
. Another blog says that at a slow pace with a guide it takes about
2 hours
, so allow extra time. The path has many pebbled steps and is shaded and cool, and from the top you can see the Sierra Madre and the Manila side.

blocks.title: Sea of Clouds and Morning Forest

children.text: If you climb the forest trail early in the morning with a guide, you may see a sea of clouds on a clear day. Starting the hike between
and
is recommended, and walking in the cool air before sunrise is best.

You can join the Dumagat (Rimontados), introduced as the original inhabitants of Mount Purro, for traditional demonstrations such as starting a fire with bamboo and cooking rice and sinigang in bamboo tubes. Always ask permission before taking photos, and confirm the experience fee when you book.

The river trek follows the stream below the reserve and is known to lead to waterfalls and a small lagoon. In the rainy season, when the water rises, it may be restricted for safety, so ask the staff about conditions on the day.

A small zipline, a high ropes course and rappelling are available, so children and beginners can try them without much pressure. Extra fees and availability change by season, so confirm when you book.

blocks.title: Pool with a Mountain View and Lounge Areas

children.text: There is a swimming pool overlooking the mountains, plus cabanas, an Asian-style lounge and bonfire areas. Soaking in the pool after a trek is the heart of a stay here.

Because the reserve is dedicated to reforestation and conservation, an eco-tourism package with tree planting and a conservation talk is offered. It suits children's education and company group activities.
Loli's Kitchen serves a Filipino home-style buffet. The food is homemade-style cooking with fresh local ingredients, and some reviews mention the papaya shake as the signature drink.

The official site describes two routes. The Sapinit Road route is shorter and easier and can be driven carefully by any vehicle, while the Boso-Boso Road route has rough paved stretches and an SUV or MPV is recommended.
Searching for the reserve's name on Waze gives directions, but it may choose a longer, harder route, so keep the written directions with you.
The last stretch includes an unpaved road, so a vehicle with good ground clearance is safer.
Road conditions can change, so it is best to ask the reservations officer to confirm your route on the day of your visit.

Purro Nature Reserve is best in the dry season, from November to May, and the booking guidance recommends December to April. The trails are drier then and the chance of a morning sea of clouds is higher.

In the rainy season from June to October, the paths turn muddy, rain is frequent and the river trek may be restricted. Rain gear and a waterproof bag are essential, and drivers should take care on the unpaved stretch.

Accommodation comes in several types: cottage, loft cottage, ground cottage, bamboo cabin, suite home, casitas, Dumagat model home, pavilion dorm and garden tent. There is no air conditioning and the mountain breeze comes in through mosquito-net windows, so bring light long sleeves and insect repellent. The dorm and tents share showers and toilets.

Meals are a Filipino home-style buffet at Loli's Kitchen. Overnight packages often include a snack, dinner and breakfast, but the contents differ by booking, so confirm them. There are almost no convenience stores or restaurants nearby, so bring snacks and water. The game room has billiards, table tennis, foosball and board games, so there is something to do on rainy days.
There is no ATM nearby, so withdraw plenty of cash in central Antipolo or Manila.
Mobile signal is relatively reliable only on some networks such as SMART and DITO, so check your carrier in advance and download an offline map.

The forest has insects and slippery sections. Use only marked trails and do not pick plants or disturb wildlife.
